hazards.attach-unpinned: That spare beater on the shelf has no retaining pin fitted. An attachment that isn't pinned to the spindle can walk up and off under load, and thirty pounds of steel coming off a spinning shaft doesn't announce which direction it's going first.
hazards.chute-bypass: You went to dump that bag straight over the top of the guard instead of through its chute. The chute is the only opening in this guard for a reason — pouring around it means your hand follows the bag right up to the edge the guard exists to keep it away from.
hazards.reach-through-guard: The guard on this mixer is propped open with a wedge instead of resting on its own interlock. A wedged guard can't do the one thing it's there for — stop the machine the instant it lifts — so reaching through it is reaching into a bowl the interlock was never actually watching.
hazards.scrape-while-running: You brought the scraper to the bowl while the beater was still turning. A 60-quart hook has enough torque to take a scraper — and the hand holding it — around with the dough. The bowl gets scraped stopped, guard open, every time, not while it's still moving.

interrupts.alert: Another baker has grabbed a scraper and is reaching straight for the bowl — the beater is still turning and they don't see it.
interrupts.cue: There's a hand headed for a moving beater and the mixer is still running.
interrupts.missNote: The reach happened anyway while the beater kept turning. A 60-quart hook does not stop for a hand that gets there first — the switch has to beat the reach, not follow it.
interrupts.why: Nobody scrapes a running bowl, and the fastest way to stop a hand that's already moving toward one is to kill the machine, not shout a warning that might land half a second too late. The stop switch is always closer than the reach is.
interrupts.wrongNote: It's the stop switch. Kill the mixer before anything else — the reach is already happening.

interrupts.alert: You feel the bowl lift's lock give a notch — the bowl has started to settle while the guard is still open and your hands are on the scraper.
interrupts.cue: The bowl underneath your hands is drifting down on its own.
interrupts.missNote: The bowl kept settling with the lock unseated and your hand still at the rim. It happened to stop before it caught anything. A lift lock that's given once is a lift lock that gives again — it gets reseated the moment it's felt, not after the stroke you're mid-way through.
interrupts.why: A lift lock that's slipped is a bowl in motion with nothing controlling it — with the guard open for the scrape-down, that's the one moment a settling bowl and a hand at the rim are sharing the same space. Re-seat the lock immediately, before the scrape continues.
interrupts.wrongNote: It's the lift lock pin — reseat it before the scraper goes back to the bowl.

lateNotes.beater: The bowl has to be up and locked before an attachment goes anywhere near the spindle.
lateNotes.scraper: Not yet — the mixer stops and the guard comes open before the scraper goes anywhere near the bowl.
lateNotes.start-switch: Not until the attachment's pinned and the speed is set from the card. Starting early runs an unproven setup at load.

name: Bakery Mixer

passRule.note: stars >= 2 and no unsafe action (WebXR/shared/records.js passed())

steps.cue: Check the bowl size, the attachment, the starting speed and the mix time.
steps.prompt: Check the bowl size, the attachment, the starting speed and the mix time.
steps.title: Read the batch card
steps.why: The card sets the attachment and the starting speed before the bowl ever goes up — a bread dough hook run at a whisk's speed tears the gluten instead of building it, and that's a wasted batch discovered only after the timer runs out.

steps.cue: Hold the guard open through the full check and confirm the beater stops dead, not coasts.
steps.holdBreakNote: Let go before the check finished. A guard test that isn't held the full count hasn't actually proven anything — hold it again.
steps.prompt: Hold the guard open through the full check and confirm the beater stops dead, not coasts.
steps.title: Prove the bowl guard interlock
steps.why: OSHA 1910.212 exists for exactly this machine: the guard is the safeguard, and a safeguard that hasn't been tested today is an assumption wearing a guard's shape. Proving it stops the beater the instant it lifts is what makes everything that follows — the chute, the scrape-down — actually safe to do the way the procedure says.

steps.cue: Turn the lift crank until the bowl reaches mixing height.
steps.prompt: Turn the lift crank until the bowl reaches mixing height.
steps.title: Raise the bowl on the lift
steps.why: The lift carries the bowl's full weight plus whatever's in it, which is exactly why it's a geared crank and not a lift by hand — a 60-quart bowl of dough is not something anybody's back should be finding out the hard way.

steps.cue: Hold the lock pin engaged until it seats fully at mixing height.
steps.holdBreakNote: Released before the pin seated. A half-caught lock looks locked and isn't — hold it through the full count.
steps.prompt: Hold the lock pin engaged until it seats fully at mixing height.
steps.title: Seat the lift lock
steps.why: A bowl held up by the crank alone can settle the moment anyone leans on it; the lock pin is what actually keeps it at height under load. It has to be held through the full seat, not bumped and let go, or the lock can catch on the first tooth instead of the last one.

steps.cue: Lift the attachment from the rack and seat it square on the spindle.

drag.missNote: Not seated on the spindle — bring the attachment up square before it goes anywhere near the shaft.

steps.prompt: Lift the attachment from the rack and seat it square on the spindle.
steps.title: Seat the attachment on the spindle
steps.why: The card named this attachment for a reason — a hook builds gluten, a paddle creams fat and sugar, and the wrong one on the spindle either tears the dough or never actually creams the batch, whatever the timer says.

steps.cue: Lock the retaining pin so the attachment can't walk off the spindle.
steps.prompt: Lock the retaining pin so the attachment can't walk off the spindle.
steps.title: Pin the attachment
steps.why: Nothing about the spindle stops an unpinned attachment from working its way upward under load — the pin is the only thing holding it down there, and it gets checked before the mixer ever starts turning, not after something sounds wrong.

steps.cue: Bring the speed dial to the card's starting figure and commit inside the band.

gauge.label: SPEED
gauge.missNote: Off the card's starting speed — reset the dial to spec before the mixer runs.

steps.prompt: Bring the speed dial to the card's starting figure and commit inside the band.
steps.title: Set the starting speed from the card
steps.why: A mixer only changes speed safely at a stop — this dial gets set once, from the card, before the start switch is ever touched, because reaching for it once the beater is already loaded and turning is how a hand ends up at the edge of a moving bowl.

steps.cue: Carry the flour bag to the chute opening and feed it through — never over the top of the guard.

drag.missNote: Not lined up with the chute — bring the bag to the opening in the guard, not over the top of it.

steps.prompt: Carry the flour bag to the chute opening and feed it through — never over the top of the guard.
steps.title: Add ingredients through the guard's chute
steps.why: The chute is the one gap this guard has, sized for a stream of flour and nothing wider than that. Dumping over the guard instead puts a hand exactly where the guard's whole job is to keep it from being.

steps.cue: Hold the start switch through the mix time on the card.
steps.holdBreakNote: Stopped short of the card's mix time. An underworked batch doesn't finish itself later — reset and run it through.
steps.prompt: Hold the start switch through the mix time on the card.
steps.title: Run the batch to the card's time
steps.why: A mixer left running past its own timer overworks the dough the same way an early stop underworks it — the card's time is the target because somebody already found out what happens on either side of it.

steps.cue: Hit the stop switch fully before the guard or the scraper comes anywhere near the bowl.
steps.prompt: Hit the stop switch fully before the guard or the scraper comes anywhere near the bowl.
steps.title: Stop the mixer before scraping down
steps.why: This is the one action that makes the next step legal at all — the beater has to be stopped, not slowing, before the guard opens. A mixer that's still coasting down is still a mixer with a moving beater in it.

steps.cue: Open the guard and run the scraper along the bowl wall in steady, controlled strokes.
steps.holdBreakNote: Stroke went ragged. Bring the scraper back to a steady, controlled pass along the wall.
steps.prompt: Open the guard and run the scraper along the bowl wall in steady, controlled strokes.
steps.title: Scrape the bowl down
steps.why: The scrape-down only happens stopped and guard open — the flip side of the rule that keeps the guard closed while the beater turns. A controlled pass along the wall gets the unmixed edges back into the batch without a hand anywhere near a beater that's still capable of moving.

steps.cue: Release the lock and turn the crank to bring the finished batch back down.
steps.prompt: Release the lock and turn the crank to bring the finished batch back down.
steps.title: Lower the bowl off the lift
steps.why: The bowl comes down the same controlled way it went up — geared, not dropped — because a full 60-quart bowl let go of partway down the crank is exactly the weight the lift exists to manage in the first place.

steps.cue: Turn the main power off and apply your lock before the guard or the bowl seal comes apart for cleaning.
steps.prompt: Turn the main power off and apply your lock before the guard or the bowl seal comes apart for cleaning.
steps.title: Lock out the mixer for the deep clean
steps.why: A between-batch scrape happens stopped; a full teardown for the deep clean happens locked out — OSHA 1910.147, the same control of hazardous energy a machine shop uses on a press brake, sized here for a mixer somebody is about to reach fully inside of.

steps.cue: Two things at this mixer are wrong. Find them by looking.

itemNames.spindle-buildup: dried dough built up on the spindle

itemNotes.chute-guard-crack: The chute's flap guard has a crack running through the hinge. It still closes, but a cracked flap is one hard knock from not closing at all.
itemNotes.spindle-buildup: Dried dough has built up around the spindle collar. Buildup there is exactly what keeps an attachment from seating flush the next time somebody pins one on.

steps.prompt: Two things at this mixer are wrong. Find them by looking.
steps.title: Walk the station before the next batch
steps.why: A guard that still closes and a spindle that still spins are not the same as a mixer that's actually ready for the next baker — the two things worth catching now are exactly the ones nobody notices until the batch after this one.

tagline: Bowl guard proven, the lift locked, the attachment pinned, ingredients through the chute, and the mixer stopped before anything comes near the bowl
